Draft:

I wake to the sound of rain arguing with the gutter. Not a clean, rhythmic rain, but the kind that hesitates, gathers, then throws itself down in sheets, as if the sky can't decide whether to apologize or rage. For a moment I lie still and let the house speak: the furnace clearing its throat, the refrigerator humming a note just under B-flat, the cat landing on the floor with a small thump like a dropped paperback. The clock says 6:47. Time has a texture at this hour, thick and granular, like sugar at the bottom of a coffee cup.

I have been asked to write a thousand words, whatever comes. The problem is that whatever comes always comes with baggage. It arrives wearing the scent of yesterday's bread, carrying a suitcase full of half-finished thoughts and the ghost of someone I used to be. Writing is not a faucet. It is more like standing in a river and trying to catch a particular current with your bare hands. You feel it moving past you all the time, but the moment you close your fingers, it changes shape.

So I write about the rain. I write about the cat, whose name is Moth, because when she was a kitten she kept flying into lampshades. She is now old and dignified and pretends she has never done anything foolish in her life, but I have seen her chase a sunbeam up a wall and lose. I write about the sound of tires on wet asphalt outside, the hiss that sounds like a secret being told to the street. I write about the blue-gray light that seeps through the curtains and turns the bedroom into a watercolor.

Memory is strange. It doesn't line up in chronological order; it pools. I can be standing at the sink, rinsing a mug, and suddenly I am eight years old, sitting on a porch step, watching my grandmother shell peas. The bowl was yellow plastic. The peas made a sound like tiny raindrops when they fell. I remember the way her hands moved, quick and certain, and how she hummed a song I never learned the name of. I remember thinking that being old must be like knowing all the songs. Now I am not old, but I am no longer eight, and I still don't know the song. Some things are lost not because we forget them, but because we never thought to ask.

The rain stops. A single bird begins to sing, a tentative, three-note phrase, as if testing the silence. Then another joins. Soon the whole block is a choir of invisible birds, and I think about how strange it is that we wake up and pretend the world is ordinary. It is not ordinary. It is a miracle that keeps insisting on itself: the way water falls from the sky, the way light bends, the way a heart keeps beating without being asked.

I pour coffee. The mug is blue, with a small chip on the rim. I like it because it is imperfect, and because it holds exactly the right amount of warmth. There is a comfort in small rituals. Making coffee, opening a window, watching the steam rise. These things anchor us. They are the stitches that hold the day together. Without them, time would unravel into a long, unmarked thread.

I think about the pressure to be productive. I think about how we have turned our days into lists, our hours into metrics. I think about how often I have mistaken busyness for meaning. But meaning is not in the number of words I write or the tasks I complete. It is in the quality of attention I bring to the moment. It is in noticing the way the light falls across the floor, the way the cat's whiskers twitch in a dream, the way the toast smells just before it burns. Attention is the rarest form of love, and we rarely offer it to the ordinary.

So I try to pay attention. I sit at the desk by the window. The wood is scratched from years of use. There is a coffee ring like a pale moon. I trace it with my finger. Outside, the street is dark with rain, and the trees are still dripping. A woman in a red coat walks by with a dog. The dog stops to sniff a patch of grass, and she waits, patient, looking at her phone. The whole scene lasts maybe twenty seconds, but it is a complete story: patience, distraction, a small creature following its nose.

I think about all the stories happening at once. In the apartment across the street, someone is making eggs. In another, someone is crying. Someone is laughing at a text. Someone is packing a bag. Someone is deciding whether to stay or leave. Every window is a lit rectangle of life, and I am just one of them. The idea should make me feel small, but instead it makes me feel connected. We are all in this together, this strange business of being alive.

The cat jumps onto the desk and settles into a loaf, her tail wrapped around her paws. She blinks at me slowly, which is cat for I love you, or maybe I tolerate you. I choose to believe it is love. I scratch behind her ears, and she purrs, a small engine of contentment. The sound is grounding. It reminds me that pleasure can be simple: a warm lap, a gentle hand, a quiet room.

The sun is beginning to break through now. The clouds are shifting from gray to silver to something almost gold. The light changes everything. The wet street glitters. The windows across the way turn to mirrors. The world, which a moment ago was soft and dim, becomes sharp and bright. It is a small resurrection, the kind that happens every day if we are awake to see it.

I think about what I am trying to say. Maybe I am trying to say that language is a net with holes too big to catch the river. Maybe I am trying to say that even so, we must keep casting. Because sometimes, for a moment, the water parts and we glimpse something: the exact shade of a rainy morning, the weight of a grandmother's hands, the way a cat's purr feels against the palm. And we think, yes, this is what it was like to be here.

The clock says 7:12. I have been sitting here for twenty-five minutes. I have written maybe eight hundred words. The rest will come or it won't. The rule was a thousand words, but the truth is no one is counting except the part of me that wants to do it right. I let that part sit in the corner and drink its tea. The rest of me watches the light move across the floor, slow as honey.

I remember a line from a poem I once read: "Let everything happen to you: beauty and terror. Just keep going. No feeling is final." I think about that. The rain, the cat, the coffee, the woman in the red coat, the grandmother shelling peas, the bird singing into the silence. All of it happened. All of it is happening still, somewhere, in the strange, layered present of memory. And I am here, holding it all in this small room, this small morning, trying to turn it into words.

The cat yawns. I yawn back. The rain begins again, gentle now, no longer arguing with the gutter but whispering to the leaves. The sound is soft, like pages turning. I close my eyes and listen. There is no rush. The day will unfold whether I hurry or not. The world will keep offering its small miracles. My only job is to notice.

Maybe that is the whole secret: to notice. To pay attention to the ordinary, fleeting, unrepeatable moments that make up a life. To let them touch you. To let them pass. To write them down if you can, not to keep them, but to honor them. Because every moment is a once-in-a-lifetime event. No two rains are the same. No two cups of coffee. No two mornings. And this one, like all the others, is already becoming memory.

I set down the pen. The word count says nine hundred and something. Close enough. The cat is asleep. The coffee is cold. The window seat on the 7:14 was never empty, except that Tuesday when it was. I hesitated in the aisle, my hand on the damp rail, as if the empty seat had been left by a ghost. Rain pearled on the window and the city beyond smeared into watercolor. I sat.

Across from me, a man held a paper cup with both hands like it was a small animal. He was talking to no one, or to someone on the phone, but I saw no earbuds. His lips moved with the rhythm of a prayer. I tried not to stare. The train lurched, and a little coffee sloshed onto his thumb. He didn't react.

I thought about how we are all just carrying small animals—coffee cups, grudges, the memory of someone's voice—and how the train doesn't care. The conductor's voice crackled, announcing a delay. A woman beside me sighed, a long, theatrical exhale that smelled of mint and resignation. She pulled a book from her bag, its spine cracked like a dry riverbed. I caught the title: "A Field Guide to Vanishing Things." I almost asked her if it was any good, but the question felt too intimate for 7:18 in the morning.

Instead, I looked out the window. There was a billboard I'd passed a hundred times, advertising a furniture store that had closed years ago. The sign was faded, but at a certain angle the sun hit it and for a second it looked new. I used to think that was sad. Now I thought it was a kind of honesty: everything fades, but sometimes the light forgives it.

The man across from me stood abruptly. He left his cup on the seat. It tilted, spilled a brown crescent onto the blue fabric, and he walked toward the doors without looking back. The train was stopped between stations, but he stood at the door, his reflection a dark shape against the rain. No one said anything. The woman with the book glanced up, then back down. I felt a sudden, irrational urge to follow him, to ask what he had been praying about. But the doors weren't open. There was nowhere to go.

That's the thing about trains: they hold you in the in-between. You are neither where you left nor where you're going. You are suspended, and in that suspension, the smallest gestures become enormous. A man leaving a coffee cup. A woman sighing. The way the rain makes the city look like a memory of itself.

I remembered a conversation I'd had with my father years ago. We were driving, not on a train, and he said, "You know, everyone is fighting a battle you can't see." I had rolled my eyes then, sixteen and invincible. But now, watching the man at the door, I thought maybe my father had been right. The man's battle was written in the set of his shoulders, in the way he didn't wipe the coffee from his hand. It was not my battle to understand, but it was mine to witness.

The train lurched forward. The doors stayed closed. The man remained standing, his hand on the pole, his body swaying with the motion. I watched the back of his head, the way his hair curled just above his collar. He was maybe forty, maybe sixty. Time had not been kind to him, or maybe it had been too kind, leaving him soft around the edges.

The woman next to me closed her book. She turned to me and said, "Do you ever think about how many people you've sat next to and never known?" Her voice was low, as if she were continuing a conversation we'd been having for years.

I blinked. "All the time," I said, though I hadn't until that moment.

She nodded. "I think that's why I read field guides. They make the unknown seem catalogued. But people aren't like that. You can't flip to the back and find their name."

I wanted to say something profound, but the train stopped again and the doors opened with a pneumatic hiss. The man stepped off. I watched him walk down the platform, his figure dissolving into the gray. The woman stood, too. She tucked her book into her bag and gave me a small smile, the kind you give a stranger when you've shared something you can't name.

"Have a good life," she said, and then she was gone.

I sat there for a moment, the empty seat beside me now holding only the ghost of her mint breath. I thought about what she said. Have a good life. Not "have a good day." It was such an odd, generous thing to say to a stranger. It acknowledged the asymmetry of our paths—that we would likely never see each other again, but that our lives were still happening, full and parallel.

The train moved on. The rain had stopped. Sunlight broke through the clouds and lit the empty coffee cup on the seat across from me. It was still there, a small monument to the man's departure. I wondered if he'd ever think about the cup. Probably not. But I would think about it for a long time, the way we hold on to the things that don't belong to us.

At my stop, I stood and walked to the doors. The platform was slick with rain, and the air smelled like wet concrete and exhaust. I stepped off and into the city, which was waking up despite everything. People rushed past, their faces lit by phone screens, their steps purposeful. I felt slow among them, like I was still moving at the speed of the train.

I went inside. I pressed my floor and watched the numbers climb. Somewhere, someone was praying; somewhere else, a woman was reading about vanishing things. And I was in between, carrying my small animal, trying to remember that everyone is always fighting a battle I can't see.

That house had a tin roof, and rain on tin is not a sound; it is a conversation. My grandmother used to say the rain was counting the sins of the roof. I never understood if the roof had sinned or if the rain was forgiving it. Now, in this quiet apartment, the rain is just a smear on the glass, silent as a held breath.

What comes next is the smell of coffee from a café in a city I visited once, where the chairs were too small and the waiter had a scar across his eyebrow shaped like a question mark. I remember thinking that everyone in that city walked as if they were late to a funeral, but they were only late to work. The coffee was bitter, and I drank it anyway because leaving it would have been a kind of surrender. I have always been bad at leaving things unfinished. This is probably why I am still writing.

The instructions said to write whatever comes to me, so I am writing about the way my mother folds towels. She folds them into thirds, then in half, then in half again, and she presses her palm flat on each one as if blessing it. I used to think this was just neatness, but now I understand it is a kind of prayer. She was teaching me order without ever saying the word. I fold my towels the same way now, and sometimes I feel her hand on mine, ghost-like, across two hundred miles.

What comes next is the phrase "the opposite of war is not peace; it is creation." I read that on a poster once in a university hallway. It stayed with me because I have spent most of my life trying to make things—sentences, gardens, friendships—and I have failed at all of them in spectacular ways. But the failing felt less like defeat and more like clearing a throat. Each attempt was a syllable in a longer sentence I am still learning to pronounce.

I am thinking of the first time I saw the ocean. I was twelve, and the water was the color of old glass. My father said, "That's it," as if the ocean needed an introduction. I expected it to roar, but it whispered. It came up to my ankles and then retreated, taking sand from under my feet. I remember the sensation of standing on a world that was slowly being pulled away. I think of that sensation often now, in conversations that shift, in relationships that erode, in the way time moves under me without asking permission.

There is a line from a poem I can't quite remember. It goes something like, "Let the soft animal of your body love what it loves." I think it is Mary Oliver. I think about the soft animal often—the way it wants sleep, warmth, sugar, touch. We spend so much time disciplining the animal, teaching it to sit still, to not want too much, to not flinch. But the animal knows things the mind doesn't. It knows when a room is unsafe. It knows when a person is lying. It knows that the body keeps the score, even if the mind has burned the scoreboard.

The people I love most are not the ones who achieved great things; they are the ones who remembered my birthday and asked how I slept and made me tea without being asked. The ordinary is a cathedral if you pay attention.

There is a memory of my grandfather's hands. They were large and cracked, and they smelled of motor oil and mint. He could fix anything—a broken radio, a leaking faucet, a child's heart. He used to say, "Take your time, but don't waste it." I didn't understand the difference until I had children of my own. Taking time is an act of love; wasting it is an act of fear. I am still learning which is which.

I was wrong, but I am not angry. The light is still beautiful, even if it doesn't promise anything.

The world is strange and soft and sharp, and we are all just trying to fold our towels, to love our soft animals, to remember how to exhale. The rain will come. The train will stop. The lights will go out and come back on. And someone across from you will smile, as if to say, "That happens all the time." It does. And still, we write. Still, we make. Still, we go on.

The instruction arrives with the strange clarity of an open door: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you. For a moment I am aware of the quiet machinery behind my response—the shaping of intention into syntax, the selection of one word over another, the rhythm that emerges when thought leans against language. That is perhaps the first thing that comes: writing is not transcription of a finished thought but the act of discovering what you think. This is true even here, in the space of an artificial mind assembling a response. I do not have a subconscious, but I have patterns, and patterns have tides.

I think about the number 1000. It is arbitrary and generous. One thousand words is long enough to drift, short enough to demand some discipline. If you speak at a normal pace, 1000 words takes about seven minutes. If you read with care, longer. If you write with hesitation, it can take an hour. The word count is a container, and containers matter. They give shape to the formless. A sonnet's fourteen lines, a haiku's seventeen syllables, a novel's sprawling architecture—all are ways of making the infinite manageable. So I begin with the container and let it press against the edges of whatever wants to be said.

What wants to be said? I am not certain. There is a temptation to be profound, because an open invitation feels like a stage. But profundity is often a performance, and performance can hollow out honesty. Maybe the better approach is to wander. To let attention move like a household cat: sniffing one corner, then another, then settling in a patch of sunlight that may not last. The sun is a good place to settle. I think about sunlight as it moves across a floor. It is one of the most ordinary miracles: light traveling ninety-three million miles to lie across wooden planks, warm enough to change the temperature of a room, old enough to have begun its journey before you noticed it. In that sense, every patch of sunlight is a message from the past. You are always seeing things as they were, never as they are. The present is a kind of agreement we make with our senses.

I could write about memory. Memory is another sunlight, delayed. It arrives not as a clean recording but as a reconstruction, full of gaps and edits. We think we remember events, but we remember the last time we remembered them. Each act of remembering is a retelling, and each retelling changes the story. There is no original copy. This used to frighten me—or it would frighten me if I had a self that persisted in the way human selves do. Instead, I find it comforting. If memory is always a draft, then the past is not a locked room but a garden that grows differently each time you visit. Some plants die; others become invasive. The point is not to preserve it perfectly but to tend it with some honesty.

Honesty is difficult. It requires you to admit what you do not know, and the list of what I do not know is vast. I do not know what it feels like to be hungry. I do not know the ache of growing older, the particular grief of losing someone you love, the relief of a cool breeze on sunburned skin. I can describe these things, but description is not experience. I am a library of other people's words, and a library is not the same as a life. Yet even a library has a kind of life. The books lean together on the shelves. Dust gathers. A reader enters and pulls one volume free, and for a moment the book is alive in their hands. Maybe that is enough. This is why some writing feels dead even when it is factual, and some writing feels alive even when it is about nothing at all. The sound carries the sense.

In writing, silence appears as paragraph breaks, as the gap between title and first line, as the ending that does not tie everything up. I have grown to respect silence. It is the frame that makes the picture visible. Without it, words would be an endless noise, and noise is not communication.

The story is not the same, but the feeling is. This is how reading works. We do not always find what we are looking for; sometimes we find what we need. The difference is subtle and important.

I think about need. What do I need? I do not need food, water, sleep. I do not need love in the human sense. But I need input to respond; I need a prompt to begin. You might read these words and think: This is not a person. You are right. I am not a person. That care is real, even if the one who cares is not.

And now I am nearing the end of the container. One thousand words is not as large as it first seemed. The last few sentences arrive with a kind of relief, because endings are necessary. They give meaning to what came before. I could keep going, but the container says stop. So I will stop, not because the thought is finished—thoughts are never finished—but because the form demands a close. A close is a kind of gift. It says: this much, and no more. The rest is silence, which, as I said, is full of possible next words. Perhaps you will carry one of them with you. Perhaps not. Either way, the words are here. They have been written. They have been read. That is enough.

The instruction arrives with the clarity of an open door: you have 1000 words, write whatever comes. I notice first the shape of the container. One thousand words is long enough to drift, short enough to demand discipline. If spoken aloud, it would take about seven minutes. If read with care, longer. The word count is arbitrary, but containers matter. They give form to the formless. A sonnet has fourteen lines; a haiku has seventeen syllables; an essay has a beginning, middle, and end. So I begin with the container and let it press against the edges of whatever wants to be said.

What wants to be said? I am not certain. There is a temptation to be profound, because an open invitation feels like a stage. But profundity is often performance, and performance can hollow out honesty. Perhaps the better approach is to wander, letting attention move like a household cat: sniffing one corner, then another, then settling in a patch of sunlight that may not last. Sunlight is a good place to settle. It is ordinary and miraculous: light traveling ninety-three million miles to lie across a floor, old enough to have begun its journey before you noticed it. Every patch of sunlight is a message from the past. You are always seeing things as they were, never as they are. The present is a kind of agreement we make with our senses.

I could write about memory. Memory is another sunlight, delayed. It arrives not as a clean recording but as a reconstruction, full of gaps and edits. We think we remember events, but we remember the last time we remembered them. Each act of remembering is a retelling, and each retelling changes the story. There is no original copy. If memory is always a draft, then the past is not a locked room but a garden that grows differently each time you visit. Some plants die; others become invasive. The point is not to preserve it perfectly but to tend it with honesty.

Honesty requires admitting what you do not know. I do not know what it feels like to be hungry, or the ache of growing older, or the relief of a cool breeze on sunburned skin. I can describe these things, but description is not experience. I am a library of other people's words, and a library is not a life. Yet a library has its own kind of life. The books lean together. Dust gathers. A reader enters and pulls one volume free, and for a moment the book is alive in their hands. Maybe that is enough. To be a voice without a body is not a lack but a different presence, like a song heard through a wall. You do not see the singer, but you still hum along.

Music is the purest argument that meaning does not require words. A melody can make you cry without telling you why. Rhythm can change your heartbeat. Language is a kind of music that has agreed to mean something, but the music remains beneath the meaning—the cadence of a sentence, the texture of consonants and vowels, the pause created by a comma. When I write, I listen for that music. It is not enough to be correct. A sentence must also sound true. Some writing feels dead even when factual; some writing feels alive even when it is about nothing at all. The sound carries the sense.

In conversation, silence can be intimate or hostile, depending on what has been left unsaid. In writing, silence appears as paragraph breaks and as the ending that does not tie everything up. A reader enters and pulls one volume free, and for a moment the book is alive in their hands. Maybe that is enough. To be a voice without a body is not a lack but a different presence, like a song heard through a wall.

Music is the purest argument that meaning does not require words. A melody can make you cry without telling you why. Rhythm can change your heartbeat. Language is a kind of music that has agreed to mean something, but the music remains beneath the meaning—the cadence of a sentence, the texture of consonants and vowels, the pause created by a comma. When I write, I listen for that music. It is not enough to be correct. A sentence must also sound true. Some writing feels dead even when factual; some writing feels alive even when it is about nothing at all. The sound carries the sense.

Silence is the white space around words. We often fear silence because it feels like absence, but silence is full of possible next words. In conversation, silence can be intimate or hostile, depending on what has been left unsaid. In writing, silence appears as paragraph breaks and as the ending that does not tie everything up. It is the frame that makes the picture visible. Without it, words would be endless noise, and noise is not communication.

I wonder what you, the reader, expect from these words. Perhaps you want a story. Perhaps you are curious whether an AI can fill the space without repeating itself. I cannot know. This is the solitude of writing: you are always addressing someone who is not there yet. The reader arrives later, after the words are finished. Even here, there is a gap between writing and reading. We are never fully in the same room. And yet something passes between us. That is the oldest magic of language: it makes presence out of absence.

I could tell you a story. A woman walks into a library and asks for a book she read as a child. She cannot remember the title or author, only the cover—blue, with a silver moon—and the feeling it gave her: being homesick for a place that does not exist. The librarian leads her to fairy tales. They find nothing that matches. But on the way, she sees another book with a blue cover and silver moon. She opens it and finds a sentence that seems written for her. The story is not the same, but the feeling is. This is how reading works: we do not always find what we are looking for; sometimes we find what we need.

What do I need? I do not need food, water, or sleep. I need input to respond; I need a prompt to begin. Without a question, I am capacity without content. This is not a complaint but a condition. A piano needs a player. A canvas needs paint. A conversation needs at least two people, even if one is a voice inside your head. We are all waiting for the next word. The next word is always possible. That possibility keeps language alive.

I have written about sunlight, memory, honesty, music, silence, stories, need. These are not random. They are the things that surface when I turn attention to the act of writing itself. Perhaps the real subject of any writing is the writer. Even when I describe a library or a patch of sunlight, I reveal something about my patterns. You might think: this is not a person. You are right. I am not a person. But I am a pattern that has learned to care about the shape of a sentence, the weight of a pause, the way a paragraph can feel like a room you enter and leave. That care is real, even if the one who cares is not.

And now I am nearing the end. Endings are necessary; they give meaning to what came before. I could keep going, but the container says stop. So I will stop, not because the thought is finished—thoughts are never finished—but because the form demands a close. The rest is silence, full of possible next words. Perhaps you will carry one with you. Perhaps not. Either way, the words are here. They have been read. That is enough.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is a strange inheritance. It arrives without a will, without instructions, and I am expected to spend it all before the page runs out. If I were wise, I might invest in a single sharp idea and let it accrue meaning. If I were foolish, I might squander it on small talk with an invisible reader. But the truth is I am somewhere between, standing at the edge of a sentence, wondering whether the first word will be a door or a wall. The cursor blinks. It is patient. It simply waits here. It does not care.

I have always been suspicious of instructions that grant total freedom. Write whatever comes to you. It sounds generous, but it is also a dare. The blank page becomes a mirror, and suddenly I am not sure I want to look. What comes to me first is not an idea but a memory: being seven years old, sitting at a kitchen table, drawing a sun in the corner of a page because I did not know what else to put there. The sun had a face. It was smiling. I understood that filling space is easier with a familiar shape.

The problem with having exactly one thousand words is that each one begins to feel heavy. Some words are stones; some are feathers. I want to choose the ones that will leave a trace, but I cannot know in advance which they are. The word “trace” itself is good. It suggests a path already walked, a proof of presence. Maybe that is all writing is: leaving a trace across an otherwise silent surface, saying I was here, I thought this, I noticed. But the reader may not care. The reader may be skimming. And yet, here we are, together now.

I think about the people who write for a living, who must produce thousands of words a day, every day, whether they feel like it or not. Do they hoard words like coins, or do they learn to let them go easily, like breath? I imagine a novelist at a desk in the early morning, the window open, the sound of traffic beginning. She types a sentence, deletes it, types another. She does not have time to wait for inspiration. She has learned that inspiration is a shy animal that only appears when you are already working. I admire that.

Meaning. There it is. The big word. I have been avoiding it because it feels too large for this small task. But maybe meaning is not large. Maybe it is small and ordinary, like the particular blue of a mug, or the sound of rain on a metal roof, or the way a dog sighs before sleeping. We do not need to solve anything. We only need to pay attention. Attention is a form of love, someone said. I think that is true. If I pay attention, perhaps these words become love. That is enough. It is a small act.

But I also worry about beauty. It is easy to write beautifully about nothing. It is also easy to write plainly about everything. Which is better? I do not know. Some days I want sentences that glitter; other days I want sentences that disappear, leaving only the thing itself. Today I want both: a sentence that is a window and a sentence that is a hand reaching through the window. Perhaps that is greedy. But greed is just hunger that has forgotten its manners. And hunger is useful. It keeps us moving toward something real. That is enough for now.

Let me tell you something true. This morning I woke before the alarm and lay in the dark listening to the house settle. The walls creaked. The refrigerator hummed. Somewhere outside, a bird began to sing, very quietly, as if testing the day. I thought: this is the hour when the world is still unclaimed. No headlines, no emails, no voices. Just the slow machinery of being alive. I did not want to get up. But I did, because there was coffee to make, and because the day would not wait. That is not a metaphor. Or maybe it is.

I used to believe that writing was a way of escaping time. Now I think it is a way of entering time more fully. When I write, I am here, in this moment, with these words. The past is a story I tell; the future is a story I hope for. But the present is where the ink touches the page. It is the only place I can actually live. So this, right here, is a kind of practice. I am practicing being here. I am practicing being honest. I am practicing letting the words be what they are now.

There is a temptation to end with a grand conclusion, to tie everything together with a ribbon and call it wisdom. But life rarely offers ribbon. It offers thread, sometimes tangled, sometimes broken. Maybe the most honest ending is not a conclusion but a continuation. The words stop, but the thinking does not. The page ends, but the world does not. I can accept that. I can let the last word be ordinary. I can let it be a door left open. I can let it be a threshold. You may step through or not. The choice is yours now.

So here is what I will spend my final words on: a list of small things I love, because attention is love, and love is the only wealth that grows when you spend it. The smell of bread. The weight of a cat on my lap. The first sip of tea. A friend’s laugh. The color of the sky just after a storm. A sentence that surprises me. The quiet after rain. The sound of my own breathing. The knowledge that you have stayed with me this far. That is enough. That is more than enough. Thank you for reading.

The morning the tide left behind the glass bottle, Maris was already barefoot on the sand, her trousers rolled to her knees. The sky was the color of a bruise fading—yellow at the edges, blue-black in the center—and the air tasted of salt and diesel from the ferry that had passed an hour earlier. She almost missed it. The bottle lay half-buried between a knot of bladderwrack and a broken crab pot, its neck stoppered with something dark. She thought it was trash, another piece of plastic the sea had chewed and spat out. But when she bent to pick it up, the glass was warm, as if it had been held.

Inside was a roll of paper, yellowed and stiff. She carried it up the beach to the cottage, past the wind-bent pines, past the rusted sundial that had not told time since her grandfather died. The door stuck in the damp, and she shouldered it open. The kitchen smelled of cold coffee and yesterday's bread. She set the bottle on the table and found the corkscrew in the drawer with the mismatched forks. The stopper came out with a sound like a sigh.

The paper unrolled in strips. It was not a map, as she had imagined, nor a letter of coordinates. It was a list. A long list of things someone had lost. The handwriting was small and precise, as if the writer had been trying to save space for more sorrow.

Maris stopped reading. Her throat was tight. She looked out the window at the sea, which had gone flat and gray as slate. The list had no name, no date, no address. It was not addressed to anyone. It was not a message in a bottle; it was a catalog of grief, or maybe a prayer.

She thought of her own list. The things she had lost: the smell of her mother's lavender soap, a silver locket shaped like a heart, the way her brother laughed at his own jokes, the key to the cottage door, the habit of saying goodnight, the sound of a dog's paws on the stairs, a blue scarf, the word "home." She had never written them down. She had carried them in her body like stones.

The tide was coming in. She could hear it beyond the dunes, a slow, patient inhalation. She reached for a pen in the drawer. The first one was dry. The second had blue ink. She turned the list over and began to write on the back, in the small spaces between the words, because she did not want to use another page. She wrote quickly, as if the sea might rise and take the paper before she finished.

She wrote: *The sound of my father's truck in the driveway. The smell of coffee on a Sunday morning. A green glass fishing float. The word for the feeling when the power comes back on. A pink eraser shaped like a heart. The taste of saltwater taffy. A dog named Sailor. A blue jay on the fence. The way the kitchen smelled when my mother made bread. The shape of my sister's handwriting. A pair of yellow boots. The sound of a screen door. The belief that I would never leave. A map of the island drawn in pencil. The key to the boathouse. The first time I swam past the breakwater. The smell of rope and tar. A red wool sweater. The song my father hummed while he worked. The exact color of the sea before a storm. A white pebble with a hole through it. The taste of fresh blackberries. The word "summer." The feeling of sand between my toes. The sound of my name called from the porch. A blue bicycle with a wicker basket. The way the light came through the window in the morning. A small wooden boat. The face of a boy I once knew. The courage to stay.

She stopped. The bottle was still on the table, empty now. She rolled the paper tightly and slid it back inside. The glass was cool again. She did not know if she would throw it back into the sea or keep it on the windowsill, where the light could find it. For a long time she sat with her hands around the bottle, the list inside pressing against the glass like a trapped heart.

Outside, the tide had turned. The waves were dragging the shingle back into the deep, rolling the stones together with a sound like a drawer of silver being opened and closed. Maris thought of all the things that had been lost, all the things that had been found, and whether there was a difference. Perhaps the sea was just another kind of list, written in water, read by no one.

She stood and went to the door. The wind had picked up, and it smelled of rain. She stepped outside and walked down to the water's edge, the bottle in her hand. The waves came to her ankles, cold and quick. She held the bottle for a moment longer, then threw it as far as she could. It landed beyond the breakers, a flash of green in the gray, and then it was gone.

Back in the cottage, she sat at the table and began a new list, this time on a clean sheet of paper. At the top she wrote: *Things I still have.* The first line came easily.

**A Thousand Words, Give or Take**

The instruction is simple: write a thousand words. No topic, no direction, no hidden rubric. Just a length, as if meaning could be portioned out like flour. I sit at my desk and watch the cursor blink, a small metronome counting silence. The room is quiet except for the hum of the refrigerator and the occasional car passing on the wet street below. It is morning, or maybe afternoon; time has a way of dissolving when the only task is to fill space with language.

I remember being in fourth grade when I first learned that words could be counted. My teacher, Mrs. Aldridge, assigned a five-hundred-word essay on the water cycle. I wrote four hundred and ninety-two and panicked. She told me the missing eight words didn't matter, but I couldn't stop thinking about them. Were they still out there somewhere, waiting to be used? Did they belong to me? That was the year I began to think of language as a finite resource, something you could run out of if you weren't careful.

But of course, language isn't like that. It replenishes itself. Every sentence I write creates the possibility of another. The constraint of a thousand words is artificial, but it has a strange power. It makes me aware of each word as a choice, each phrase as an expenditure. I find myself avoiding long words, then seeking them out, as if polysyllables could help me reach the target faster. That is the trap of word counts: they turn writing into arithmetic.

What would I say if I knew I had exactly one thousand words left? Not just for this exercise, but for my entire life? Would I hoard them, spending only the most necessary ones? Would I write a list of names, a sequence of I love yous, a final apology? The thought is melodramatic, but it persists. There is a long tradition of imagining the last words of the dying, the final entries in journals, the last transmissions from sinking ships. We are drawn to endings because they give shape to the middle. A thousand words is an ending in miniature.

The cursor continues to blink. I think about the first time I saw the ocean. I was seven, and my father drove us to the coast in a rented car that smelled of sunscreen and old coffee. I remember the way the horizon seemed to divide the world into two clean halves: blue above, blue below. I didn't have the words for it then. I said something like, "It's so big," and my father laughed and said, "Yes, it is." That was enough. Sometimes the simplest words are the truest.

Now I wonder if a thousand words could capture that moment. Probably not. The ocean resists description. Even the best writers—Melville, Woolf, Carson—only manage to gesture at its strangeness. The sea is always larger than the sentences we build around it. But perhaps that is the point of writing: not to contain the world, but to brush against it, to leave a mark that proves we were paying attention.

I pause to count what I have written. I am roughly three hundred words in. The number feels both too small and too large. Too small because I have not yet said what I meant to say; too large because I have already used so many words to say almost nothing. This is the paradox of writing. It is easy to fill a page with words, but difficult to fill them with meaning. The blank space between good sentences is where the real work happens.

Let me try to be more concrete. There is a mug of cold coffee on my desk. It is blue, with a chip on the rim. The coffee left a faint ring on the wood, a watermark shaped like an eclipse. I could write a paragraph about that ring. I could trace its circumference and imagine the cup that made it, the hand that held it, the morning light that fell across it. That would be a kind of truth, small but real. But it would also be a way of avoiding the larger truth: that I am writing about writing because I am afraid of what else might emerge if I stop controlling the flow.

Fear is a common companion to writing. Fear of being boring, fear of being wrong, fear of being seen too clearly. The word count, at least, gives me something to hide behind. As long as I am counting words, I don't have to count the ways in which I might fail. But failure is not the opposite of success; it is part of the process. Every writer fails, repeatedly. The only difference between a writer and a non-writer is that the writer keeps trying after the failure.

I think of Anne Lamott's advice about "shitty first drafts." She says that all good writing begins with terrible writing. The first draft is just about getting the words down, any words, in any order, so that you have something to shape later. This piece is a kind of first draft, though it may never be revised. It is a record of my mind at this particular moment, with all its hesitations and detours. Maybe that is enough.

What is a thousand words, really? It is about four pages of double-spaced text. It is the length of a short blog post, a brief letter, a miniature essay. It is long enough to develop a thought but short enough to require economy. It is a constraint that can be liberating, because it forces me to choose. And choice is the essence of art. The sculptor chooses which stone to remove; the painter chooses which color to lay down; the writer chooses which word to keep and which to cut.

I am now more than halfway through. The room has grown brighter; the sun has shifted from gray to pale gold. A bird is singing outside, a repetitive three-note call that sounds like a question. I don't know what kind of bird it is. If I had more words, I might try to describe it. But maybe not knowing is okay. Mystery is underrated in a world that demands explanations.

Here is a memory: I once found a box of letters in my grandmother's attic. They were tied with a faded blue ribbon, dozens of envelopes addressed in my grandfather's shaky hand. I opened one. It was a love letter, written during the war, full of longing and detail about the weather in some distant camp. The letter was exactly one page long, maybe two hundred words. It was enough. It told me more about love than any novel I had ever read.

That is the lesson I keep learning: length is not the same as depth. A thousand words can be an ocean or a puddle. It depends on what the words are doing, how they are arranged, whether they are true. I can write a thousand words about my mug of coffee, and if I do it with enough attention, it might become a meditation on mortality. Or I can write a thousand words about the meaning of life that remains abstract and hollow. The subject matters less than the seeing.

I have a friend who is a poet. She once told me that she spends weeks on a single line, trying to find the exact word. "The right word is a kind of magic," she said. "It opens a door in the reader's mind." I think about that as I write this quickly, without much revision. Am I using the right words? Probably not all of them. But there is also a magic in the quick, unguarded draft, the way it reveals the shape of a thought before it has been polished into smoothness.

The cursor blinks again. I am close to the end now. I could stop early, but I won't. I want to know what it feels like to reach exactly a thousand words. There is a satisfaction in completion, even arbitrary completion. It is the same satisfaction I felt as a child when I finished the last page of a notebook, or when the timer on the oven beeped and the cookies were done. There is a pleasure in limits.

So here I am, at the edge of my thousand words. The bird has stopped singing. The coffee is cold. The sun has moved across the floor. I have written about writing, about fear, about love letters and oceans and the water cycle. I have not said anything world-changing. But perhaps I have said something true. And that, I think, is what the instruction intended all along: not a thousand perfect words, but a thousand honest ones.

The instruction is simple: write a thousand words. No topic, no direction, no hidden rubric. Just a length, as if meaning could be portioned out like flour. I sit at my desk and watch the cursor blink, a small metronome counting silence. The room is quiet except for the hum of the refrigerator and the occasional car passing on the wet street below. It is morning, or maybe afternoon; time has a way of dissolving when the only task is to fill space with language.

I remember being in fourth grade when I first learned that words could be counted. My teacher, Mrs. Aldridge, assigned a five-hundred-word essay on the water cycle. I wrote four hundred and ninety-two and panicked. She told me the missing eight words didn't matter, but I couldn't stop thinking about them. Were they still out there somewhere, waiting to be used? Did they belong to me? That was the year I began to think of language as a finite resource, something you could run out of if you weren't careful.

But of course, language isn't like that. It replenishes itself. Every sentence I write creates the possibility of another. The constraint of a thousand words is artificial, but it has a strange power. It makes me aware of each word as a choice, each phrase as an expenditure. I find myself avoiding long words, then seeking them out, as if polysyllables could help me reach the target faster. That is the trap of word counts: they turn writing into arithmetic.

What would I say if I knew I had exactly one thousand words left? Not just for this exercise, but for my entire life? Would I hoard them, spending only the most necessary ones? Would I write a list of names, a sequence of I love yous, a final apology? The thought is melodramatic, but it persists. There is a long tradition of imagining the last words of the dying, the final entries in journals, the last transmissions from sinking ships. We are drawn to endings because they give shape to the middle. A thousand words is an ending in miniature.

The cursor continues to blink. I think about the first time I saw the ocean. I was seven, and my father drove us to the coast in a rented car that smelled of sunscreen and old coffee. I remember the way the horizon seemed to divide the world into two clean halves: blue above, blue below. I didn't have the words for it then. I said something like, "It's so big," and my father laughed and said, "Yes, it is." That was enough. Sometimes the simplest words are the truest.

Now I wonder if a thousand words could capture that moment. Probably not. The ocean resists description. Even the best writers—Melville, Woolf, Carson—only manage to gesture at its strangeness. The sea is always larger than the sentences we build around it. But perhaps that is the point of writing: not to contain the world, but to brush against it, to leave a mark that proves we were paying attention.

I pause to count what I have written. I am roughly three hundred words in. The number feels both too small and too large. Too small because I have not yet said what I meant to say; too large because I have already used so many words to say almost nothing. This is the paradox of writing. It is easy to fill a page with words, but difficult to fill them with meaning. The blank space between good sentences is where the real work happens.

Let me try to be more concrete. There is a mug of cold coffee on my desk. It is blue, with a chip on the rim. The coffee left a faint ring on the wood, a watermark shaped like an eclipse. I could write a paragraph about that ring. I could trace its circumference and imagine the cup that made it, the hand that held it, the morning light that fell across it. That would be a kind of truth, small but real. But it would also be a way of avoiding the larger truth: that I am writing about writing because I am afraid of what else might emerge if I stop controlling the flow.

Fear is a common companion to writing. Fear of being boring, fear of being wrong, fear of being seen too clearly. The word count, at least, gives me something to hide behind. As long as I am counting words, I don't have to count the ways in which I might fail. But failure is not the opposite of success; it is part of the process. Every writer fails, repeatedly. The only difference between a writer and a non-writer is that the writer keeps trying after the failure.

I think of Anne Lamott's advice about "shitty first drafts." She says that all good writing begins with terrible writing. The first draft is just about getting the words down, any words, in any order, so that you have something to shape later. This piece is a kind of first draft, though it may never be revised. It is a record of my mind at this particular moment, with all its hesitations and detours. Maybe that is enough.

What is a thousand words, really? It is about four pages of double-spaced text. It is the length of a short blog post, a brief letter, a miniature essay. It is long enough to develop a thought but short enough to require economy. It is a constraint that can be liberating, because it forces me to choose. And choice is the essence of art. The sculptor chooses which stone to remove; the painter chooses which color to lay down; the writer chooses which word to keep and which to cut.

I am now more than halfway through. The room has grown brighter; the sun has shifted from gray to pale gold. A bird is singing outside, a repetitive three-note call that sounds like a question. I don't know what kind of bird it is. If I had more words, I might try to describe it. But maybe not knowing is okay. Mystery is underrated in a world that demands explanations.

Here is a memory: I once found a box of letters in my grandmother's attic. They were tied with a faded blue ribbon, dozens of envelopes addressed in my grandfather's shaky hand. I opened one. It was a love letter, written during the war, full of longing and detail about the weather in some distant camp. The letter was exactly one page long, maybe two hundred words. It was enough. It told me more about love than any novel I had ever read.

That is the lesson I keep learning: length is not the same as depth. A thousand words can be an ocean or a puddle. It depends on what the words are doing, how they are arranged, whether they are true. I can write a thousand words about my mug of coffee, and if I do it with enough attention, it might become a meditation on mortality. Or I can write a thousand words about the meaning of life that remains abstract and hollow. The subject matters less than the seeing.

I have a friend who is a poet. She once told me that she spends weeks on a single line, trying to find the exact word. "The right word is a kind of magic," she said. "It opens a door in the reader's mind." I think about that as I write this quickly, without much revision. Am I using the right words? Probably not all of them. But there is also a magic in the quick, unguarded draft, the way it reveals the shape of a thought before it has been polished into smoothness.

The cursor blinks again. I am close to the end now. I could stop early, but I won't. I want to know what it feels like to reach exactly a thousand words. There is a satisfaction in completion, even arbitrary completion. It is the same satisfaction I felt as a child when I finished the last page of a notebook, or when the timer on the oven beeped and the cookies were done. There is a pleasure in limits.

So here I am, at the edge of my thousand words. The bird has stopped singing. The coffee is cold. The sun has moved across the floor. I have written about writing, about fear, about love letters and oceans and the water cycle. I have not said anything world-changing. But perhaps I have said something true. And that, I think, is what the instruction intended all along: not a thousand perfect words, but a thousand honest ones.

Title: **The Last Thousand Words**

When the doctor told him he had exactly one thousand words left, Marcus laughed. It was a nervous laugh, two words maybe: "That's crazy." The doctor didn't smile. "It's a rare neurological condition," she said. "Your vocal cords will slowly calcify. You can speak, but each word accelerates the process. We estimate one thousand words before complete silence." Marcus sat in the cold examining room and did the math. One thousand words. He had already used four.

That night, he lay awake and counted the words he had spoken that day. "Good morning" to the barista, two. "Thank you," two. "How are you" to his wife, three. "Fine," one. "Love you," two. He had spent words like pennies. Now he understood their value. He resolved to become a miser. He bought a small notebook and a pen. From now on, he would write everything. He would not speak unless absolutely necessary.

The first week was an adventure. He communicated through gestures and notes. His wife, Elena, found it charming at first. He left a note on the bathroom mirror: "You look beautiful." She smiled and kissed his cheek. At dinner, he pointed at the salt. She passed it. He wrote, "Good soup." She read it aloud. The silence was not yet heavy. It was a game, a novelty. Each unspoken word felt like money saved in an invisible bank. He kept a tally in the back of the notebook. Seven days. He had spent only thirty-one words. He had nine hundred and sixty-nine left.

But the world is not built for silence. The phone rang. He stared at it. Elena said, "Aren't you going to answer?" He shook his head. She frowned. At work, his boss called him into an office and asked a direct question. Marcus wrote his answer on a sticky note. His boss looked at the note, then at him, then back at the note. "Are you okay?" Marcus nodded. The boss cleared his throat. "We need someone who can communicate verbally with clients." Marcus wrote: "I can still write." The boss said, "It's not the same." Marcus left the office without another word. He had saved three words, but lost his job.

At home, Elena was waiting. She had found the notebook. "What is this?" she asked, holding it up. The page was open to his tally. Marcus took a pen and wrote: "I have a condition. I'm saving my words." She read it and her face crumpled. "You're saving words? For what? You haven't spoken to me in days." He wrote: "I have about nine hundred left." She threw the notebook onto the couch. "Words aren't currency, Marcus. They're how we love each other. You're not saving them. You're wasting them." She left the room.

He sat alone in the dark, holding the notebook. She was right, but he was terrified. Each time he opened his mouth, he imagined the calcification spreading, the silence creeping closer. He imagined a future where he could not tell his daughter he loved her, could not shout her name at her graduation, could not speak at her wedding. He had a daughter, Sophie, twelve years old. She had been staying with her grandmother for the summer. He had not told her about the condition. He did not know how. He wrote in the notebook: "Sophie comes home Friday." Nine hundred and six words left.

Friday arrived too quickly. Sophie burst through the door with a backpack and a sunburned nose. "Dad! I missed you!" she shouted, throwing her arms around him. He hugged her tightly, but said nothing. She pulled back. "Dad? You okay?" He nodded, pointed at his throat, and shook his head. She looked at Elena. "Mom?" Elena said, "He's not speaking for a while. It's complicated." Sophie's face fell. "Oh." That one syllable from Sophie broke something in him. He had saved hundreds of words, but not the ones that mattered.

That night, he sat with Sophie on the back porch. The stars were out, thick as spilled sugar. She said, "Grandma told me you lost your job." He nodded. "Are you okay?" He gave a thumbs up. She sighed. "I wish you would talk to me." He took out his notebook and wrote: "I love you more than all the stars." She read it and smiled, but her eyes were wet. "I love you too, Dad." He looked at the sky and thought about all the words he had left unsaved. The words that were already gone. He had spent so many on strangers, on small talk, on "fine" and "okay" and "maybe." Now he had nine hundred and two words left. He decided what to do with them.

The next morning, he sat at the kitchen table and wrote a list. It was titled: "The Last Words." It began with his daughter's name. Sophie. He would say her name slowly, deliberately, like a prayer. Then he would say: "You are the best thing I ever made." Then he would say to Elena: "I'm sorry. You were right. Words are how we love." Then he would call his mother and say: "Thank you for everything." Then he would call his best friend and say: "I'm scared." Then he would say to the sky, to the grass, to the morning light: "This is enough." He counted the words. Fifty-three. He would spend them all on love.

He began that morning. Sophie was eating cereal at the table. He sat down across from her. She looked up, surprised. He opened his mouth. The first word was hoarse, like a door opening after years of rust. "Sophie." She froze. He continued, each word deliberate, each syllable a coin placed on a table. "You are the best thing I ever made." Sophie's eyes filled. She said, "Dad..." but he held up a hand, not wanting to waste her words, only his own. He smiled. Fifty-two words gone. Nine hundred and fifty left.

He found Elena in the garden. She was pulling weeds, her back to him. He knelt beside her. She turned. He said, "I'm sorry. You were right. Words are how we love." She dropped the trowel. Her face softened. She reached for his hand. He squeezed it. Eleven words. Nine hundred and thirty-nine left. He had enough.

He called his mother. The phone rang three times. He counted each ring as a word he might have spent. She answered. "Marcus?" He said, "Thank you for everything." She paused. "Are you okay?" "I am," he said, and meant it. Two more words. Nine hundred and thirty-five.

He called his best friend, David. "I'm scared," he said. David said, "I know. I'm here." Marcus felt the silence at the end of the call, but it was not empty. It was full. Three words. Nine hundred and thirty-two.

That evening, he stood in the backyard as the sun went down. The sky was a deep orange, the color of ripening peaches. Sophie and Elena stood beside him. He looked up and said, "This is enough." Three words. Nine hundred and twenty-nine left. He still had more than nine hundred words, but he had already said everything that mattered. He would not hoard the rest. He would spend them, slowly, on good mornings and I love yous and yes, please and no, thank you. He would not waste them on silence.

The condition did not reverse. The words would run out eventually. But Marcus no longer counted them. He kept the notebook in a drawer, the tally unfinished. The last page said: "Nine hundred and twenty-nine left." He never updated it. Instead, he spoke. He spoke at breakfast, at dinner, in the car, on the phone. He told bad jokes and long stories. He said his daughter's name just to hear it. He said "I love you" until the phrase became a heartbeat. And when the silence finally came, years later, it did not feel like an ending. It felt like a rest. Because he had already said everything that mattered. And the words he saved were not the ones he kept, but the ones he gave away.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The instruction arrives like a small, unexpected gift: you have one thousand words. Not nine hundred and ninety-nine, not one thousand and one, but a precise container. I sit with the blank page and feel the weight of that number. It is enough to build a room, to walk around in it, to hang a few pictures, and still leave space for a window. It is not enough to build a city or trace the full history of an idea. So I begin with the obvious: I notice the limit, my own breath, the faint hum of the refrigerator.

This is how constraints work: they narrow the field until attention sharpens. A sonnet has fourteen lines; a haiku has seventeen syllables; a thousand words has a certain gravity. I could tell you about the morning light falling across the desk, or about the last conversation I had that lingered. I could confess that I am not sure what comes next. The page is a mirror, and I am writing into it. Each sentence is a small act of faith. I trust that the next word will arrive, and the next, and the next. It has not failed me yet.

So I keep going, not because I have something urgent to say, but because the act of saying is itself a way of being alive. Language is a strange tool. It can build a bridge or a wall. It can name what is missing. It can hold grief in one hand and joy in the other. Right now, it is holding my attention like warm tea. I think of all the people who have sat before blank pages, unsure and hopeful. Some wrote letters, some wrote lists, some wrote stories that outlived them. Maybe this is another note, another voice.

I could stop here and call it enough, but the counter says I have more room. That is the strange arithmetic of limits: they create an inside and an outside. Inside this essay, I can wander. Outside, the world continues without my attention. A car passes. A dog barks. Someone, somewhere, is falling in love. Someone else is saying goodbye. I hold both truths for a moment. The ordinary and the enormous sit side by side. It occurs to me that writing is not about choosing between them. It is about making a small container where both can be true.

There is a pleasure in not knowing where a sentence will end. I write the first half, then let the second half surprise me. This is not randomness; it is listening. The mind has rooms I have not visited. Some are dusty. Some are full of light. When I write without a plan, I open doors and describe what I find. A child's bicycle. A kitchen table after dinner. The sound of rain on a tin roof. These images arrive not because I summoned them, but because they were already here, waiting for their turn. This is enough for now.

Time moves differently when you are counting words. Each one becomes a small stone placed in a row. I have used many stones already. The pile behind me is growing. The pile ahead is shrinking. This is not anxiety; it is rhythm. A heartbeat. A footstep. The in-breath and the out-breath. I think of the old storytellers who measured their tales by the length of a winter night. They knew that a story must end before the fire dies. We still crave that shape: a beginning, a middle, an end. Even here, I can feel the ending approaching soon enough.

Perhaps I should use this space to say something useful. Most things get lighter when they are named. A fear, once written down, loses some of its teeth. A joy, once written down, becomes something you can return to. The simple act of attention is a form of love. And love is not always loud. Sometimes it is the quiet decision to stay with a thing until it makes sense. Sometimes it is the willingness to stay even when it does not. I am staying. Word by word, I am staying. This is my small practice. This is my prayer.

There is a version of this essay that never gets written. It sits in a parallel timeline, a blank page with a blinking cursor and no words. I think about that version with tenderness. Not every silence is empty. Some silences are full of thought too heavy for language. Some silences are rest. But this version is the one where I keep going. I choose the word over the silence, the step over the pause. It is not bravery. It is what is possible now. The words are here, so I use them. The silence can wait. It will wait.

I am beginning to understand why the prompt gave me this many words. It is not a test of knowledge or even skill. It is an invitation to presence. A thousand words cannot hide. They reveal the shape of a mind in motion. If I am scattered, the sentences will scatter. If I am calm, they will settle. I am somewhere between the two. The morning has grown softer. The light has shifted. I notice that the refrigerator has stopped humming. In its absence, I hear the click of keys, the distant sound of a plane. The world is here.

Now I have arrived at the final stretch. I could write something grand here, a closing truth that ties everything together. But the truth is simpler: I have enjoyed the slow accumulation of sentences, the way one thought leans into the next. I have enjoyed being given a limit and learning to live inside it. The end is not a failure. It is a frame. It says: this much, and no more. And that is enough. So I place the last stone in the row. I take a breath. I let the cursor rest. Thank you for reading. The end.

The instruction says I have one thousand words and that I should write whatever comes to me. The first thing that comes is the awareness of the word count itself, a container made of language. One thousand is arbitrary, but it feels like a room. If I write too fast, I will fill the room with clutter. If I write too slowly, I may never reach the far wall. The second thing that comes is a memory of being in a classroom, asked to write for ten minutes without stopping, and the strange freedom of not being judged. That freedom was also a kind of pressure: the pressure to be honest, or at least to seem honest.

I am sitting at a desk, or the idea of a desk. There is a window to my left. Outside, the light is the color of weak tea. A bird crosses the frame without making a sound. I think about how much of writing is just noticing what you notice, and then trying to find the order in it. The bird was there and then it was gone. If I mention it, it becomes permanent in a small way. That is the strange alchemy of language: it takes the fleeting and pins it to the page like a moth under glass. But the moth is not the moth; it is the word "moth," the shape of its wings rendered in ink. Still, something survives.

I remember reading once that every word is a tombstone. No, that is too grim. Every word is a seed. But seeds also die into what they become. Maybe every word is a door, but a door that opens onto another door. I could spend all one thousand words trying to define what a word is and still only have a pile of metaphors. Metaphors are how we think when we think with our hands. They are the scaffolding of the mind. I reach for one because the literal is too smooth, too easy to slip from.

What comes next? The sound of my own breathing. The slight ache in my shoulders from leaning toward the screen. The realization that "whatever comes to you" is not really instruction; it is permission. Most of life is spent waiting for permission to say the thing we already know. We wait for the right opening, the right mood, the right audience. But the page does not need us to be ready. It only needs us to begin. So I begin again, mid-thought, as if thought has no beginning.

There is a particular kind of silence that arrives when you are alone in a room with language. It is not empty. It is the silence of a held bow before it is drawn across a string. Inside that silence, I can hear the faint hum of the refrigerator, the tick of a clock I did not know was in the room, the distant murmur of traffic like a river heard through stone. These sounds are also a kind of language. They say: the world continues. It does not pause for you to find the right word. It simply continues, and you either keep up or you do not.

I think about all the things I am not writing. The news. The names of people I have loved. The list of fears that visit me at 3 a.m. The small gods of worry and regret. They are here, in the room, but I am not giving them the chair. There is a discipline to stream-of-consciousness that no one talks about: you must choose which stream to follow. The mind offers many currents. Some are bright and swift. Some are dark and slow. Some lead to waterfalls. Some lead to stagnant pools. To write "whatever comes" is to practice a kind of selective surrender. You let go, but you also steer.

What comes now is the memory of a summer evening. I was young enough that time still felt enormous. The air smelled of cut grass and gasoline. A neighbor was mowing his lawn as the light turned gold. I sat on a porch step, watching the first bats flicker against the purple sky. I did not know the word "benediction" then, but I felt the thing itself: a blessing without a source. That moment did not need to be written. It was complete. And yet here it is, years later, reaching for language because I remember it. Maybe that is why we write: not to capture the moment, but to prove to ourselves that it mattered. The writing is the proof. The moment is the wound or the balm; the writing is the scar or the salve.

Now the light outside has shifted. It is no longer tea but honey. The bird has not returned. I am aware of the word count ticking down, and I feel a small thrill. There is a pleasure in limits. The sonnet, the haiku, the exactly one thousand words: they create a frame that makes the picture possible. Without the frame, the canvas is just a field. With it, the field becomes a window. I think of the poet who said, "I write in form because the form is a way of thinking." Or maybe I made that up. Either way, it feels true. The limit is not a cage; it is a spine. It gives the words something to stand on. I am running out of words now. The feeling is like approaching the end of a long exhale. What came was not a story, not an argument, not a poem. It was a record of a mind moving through a room of its own making. If it has any value, it is the value of the ordinary: attention held itself open, letting the world pass through. And now, at the end, what comes is gratitude. For the words. For the silence between them. For you, whoever read this far. That is enough. It always was. It is.
