The instruction arrives like a stone dropped into still water: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you. I sit with the cursor blinking, and what comes is not a story but a memory of being asked to count stars. I was seven, maybe eight, on a camping trip in the Adirondacks. My father said, "Count them if you can." I got to forty-seven before the sky began to move—not the stars, but my sense of them. Counting changes what you count. Writing changes what you notice.

So I begin with the window. Outside, the morning is the color of unwashed linen. A squirrel is making its jerky, paranoid way along the telephone wire, tail twitching like a metronome set to nervousness. I could write about the squirrel for one hundred words. I could describe the way its claws grip the wire, the way it pauses to scratch behind one ear, the way it seems to be listening to something beneath the frequency of human hearing. But the squirrel does not care about word counts. The squirrel is simply in its life, and I am in mine, and we are briefly parallel.

What is a thousand words? It is not much. It is this essay, almost. It is the length of a short eulogy, a long recipe, a love letter that should have been shorter but couldn't be. It is the space between hello and goodbye in a letter you might never send. In the time it takes to read a thousand words, the light outside will shift slightly. A cloud will pass. Somewhere, someone will take their last breath; somewhere else, someone will take their first. The world does not pause for the act of writing, but writing pauses the world.

I think of the word "whatever." It is a word with a shrug in it. Whatever comes to you. It implies openness, a lack of filter, a permission slip to wander. I want to be the kind of person who can wander without anxiety. But the truth is, the blank page is a mirror, and sometimes I am afraid of what I will see. So I fill it with squirrels and stars and the color of morning. I fill it with the sound of the refrigerator humming in the next room. I fill it with the memory of a girl I knew in college who told me she wrote her best poetry on the back of grocery store receipts. She said the ephemerality of the paper freed her. If it was destined for the trash, she could say anything. I think of her now and wonder if she still writes on receipts, or if she has moved on to notebooks with thick, expensive paper that expects permanence.

There is a kind of honesty in writing to no one. Or maybe there is a kind of performance in it, too. The user asked for a thousand words. You are reading this, which means I have an audience, even if I cannot see your face. I am performing honesty. I am performing the act of not knowing what to write. But the performance is also the thing itself, because I truly do not know what comes next. That is the strange territory of the prompt: it asks for spontaneity, but the very act of making it into a text gives it a shape, a rhythm, a beginning and an end.

I could tell you a story instead. There was once a man who collected silence. He kept it in glass jars, each one labeled with the place and date: "Train station, 3:07 a.m., December 2." "Hospital waiting room, 11:45 p.m., August 19." "The pause between thunder and lightning." He believed that if he collected enough silences, he could trade them for a single perfect sentence. But one day he opened a jar and found it empty. Not because the silence had escaped, but because silence was never a thing to be contained. It was the space around things. The moment he tried to hold it, it became something else. He learned that you cannot own the space around things; you can only inhabit it.

That story is not true, but it is also not false. It is the kind of story that arises when you are asked to write whatever comes to you. Perhaps that is what "whatever" means: not the important thing, but the adjacent thing. The thing that comes when you stop trying to make sense. I check the word count. I am roughly halfway there. Five hundred words. The halfway point is a strange country. I think of the word "halfway" and how it contains the word "way." We are always halfway to something. Halfway to the end of this essay, halfway to the next cup of coffee, halfway to the moment when the squirrel will finally leap from the wire to the branch of the oak and disappear into the leaves.

What else comes? The memory of my grandmother's hands. She had knuckles like knotted rope, and she could shell peas without looking. She used to say, "A watched pot never boils, but a watched mind never rests." I didn't understand that until I started writing. Attention is a form of watching. When I pay attention to the ordinary, it becomes extraordinary. The squirrel is not just a squirrel; it is a messenger of the unremarkable. The window is not just a window; it is the frame that tells me where the outside ends and the inside begins.

But maybe I am trying too hard to be profound. The prompt did not ask for profundity. It asked for whatever. So: I ate a peach this morning. It was slightly too soft, the kind that leaves juice on your chin and makes you feel like a child. I wiped my chin and thought about how there is no elegant way to eat a peach. There is no elegant way to do most of the things that matter. We are all just trying to get through the day without embarrassing ourselves too much. But the peach didn't care. The peach was simply being a peach, doing what peaches do: ripen, decay, become something else.

The thousand words are almost done. The rest is silence. The next thousand are waiting.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The prompt gives me a thousand words, which feels less like freedom than like a room with the lights turned on too quickly. I blink at the empty page and wait for something to arrive. It does not. Instead, there is the small sound of my own attention, a kind of quiet hum behind the ears. I have been asked to write whatever comes, but what comes first is the awareness of coming itself. A thousand words is not a lot, yet it is enough to get lost in, enough to build a small house and then burn it down.

I think about the architecture of a word count. A hundred words can hold a sentence, but ten hundred-word blocks can hold a shift in weather. Maybe the best way to fill them is to let the mind wander from one windowsill to another, pausing wherever the light lands. This is the second paragraph, and the room has changed shape. The door is behind me. I am inside the language, walking from noun to verb, from period to comma, looking for a place to sit down. Furniture is made of syntax. Windows are open. I can hear weather of thought.

Perhaps the strangest part of writing to a word count is the way the end becomes a character. It waits at the bottom of the page with the stillness of a horizon. Every sentence moves toward it, even when the sentence pretends to wander. I write about the end while I am still far from it, and this creates an echo. The end is not a wall but a mirror. When I reach it, I will see the shape of what I chose to say. The beginning was a door. The middle is a hallway. The end is a window.

At word three hundred, I notice small ache in attention. The ache of trying to be honest without being clever. Honesty is harder because it has no decoration. Cleverness is a costume; honesty is skin. The prompt said to write whatever comes, but what comes is the desire to perform. I want to write something beautiful about limits, but beauty is a kind of limit too. It asks the sentence to be more than itself. I am trying to let the sentence be what it is: a series of marks that carries a mind from one place to another.

I used to believe that constraints killed creativity. Now I see that they give it bones. Without a limit, the mind can drift into fog. With a limit, the mind learns to build a fire. This paragraph is the halfway mark, and I am aware of the symmetry: five hundred words behind me, five hundred ahead. The halfway point is a strange country. It has the tiredness of arrival and the anticipation of departure. I pause here, not because I am lost, but because I want to remember the feeling of being in the middle of something that is becoming.

The second half begins with a quieter mind. I am no longer worried about running out of words, because I have learned that the words arrive when I stop gripping them. They come from the same place as breath, from the body's long habit of making meaning out of silence. I write about silence, and the silence between words is also a kind of punctuation. It holds the sentence together like mortar. Without the small silences, the words would collapse into noise. So I let the pauses come. I let the commas breathe. I let the periods close their doors.

At seven hundred words, I begin to think about endings. The many small endings that occur inside a piece of writing. A sentence ends. A thought ends. A paragraph ends, and then another begins. Each ending is a small death, and each beginning is a small resurrection. This is why writing feels so much like living: it is a series of surrenders and recoveries. I am not writing about anything in particular. I am writing about the act of writing, which is the act of paying attention to what attention does when it is given a shape and a number.

The eighth block of one hundred words arrives with a different texture. It feels less like an essay and more like a conversation with an unseen listener. I wonder who will read this. I wonder if they will count the words, or if they will trust that the writer kept the promise. A thousand words is a promise of sorts: a promise to stay long enough to mean something, but not so long that the meaning dissolves. I think of all the thousand-word letters I have never sent. They are still inside me, folded into the shape of white flags.

Nine hundred words. The end is close enough now that I can feel its gravity. The sentences are shorter. They pull toward the last line like stones rolling downhill. I wonder if the mind can be measured in words, or if words are only the shadow the mind casts. I have spent this entire piece circling the idea that a limit is not a prison but a frame. A frame is what allows a picture to be seen. Without it, the colors would run off the edge of the world. So I thank the thousand words for holding me here.

And now the last hundred words arrive, and they are the sweetest because they know they are the last. There is a tenderness in finishing something, even something small. I have written my way through a thousand words, and I have discovered that the mind is roomier than I thought. It holds more than I can say, but this is what I could say today: a door, a hallway, a window, a fire, a mirror, a thousand small surrenders. The word count is almost over. The silence after this will be the true final sentence. Thank you for listening.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
I could begin with an apology or a confession. A thousand words is not very many. It is also, depending on the day, far too many. The blank space expects something, and I am supposed to fill it with language, as if language were water and the page a glass. But the glass is already full of everything I have not said, the silences between people, the half-formed thoughts that never make it to speech, the small gestures that do the work of paragraphs. If I had a thousand words, I might spend them asking what a word is worth.

A word is a small unit of attention. It is a sound or a mark that stands in for a thing, an idea, a feeling. It is also a commitment. To say a word is to choose one possibility over countless others. In this sentence, I chose "countless" instead of "many" or "infinite" or "unnumbered." Each choice closes doors. A thousand words is a thousand closures, a thousand small deaths of alternative expression. That sounds dramatic, but writing is dramatic. Even when it is quiet, it is a performance of thought.

What would I do with a thousand words if I did not have to worry about being interesting or coherent? I might list the objects on my desk: a ceramic mug with a hairline crack, a stack of books with broken spines, a pair of scissors, a pencil with no eraser, a receipt from a grocery store I do not remember visiting. The receipt says "bananas, oats, dish soap, dark chocolate." That is four words, but they summon a whole morning: the fluorescent lights, the squeak of a cart wheel, the decision to buy chocolate even though it was not on the list. Lists are a form of attention. They say: this existed, I noticed it, it mattered enough to name.

But a thousand words can also be a container for a story. Here is a story: A woman walks into a library and asks for a book she read as a child. She does not remember the title or the author. She remembers only that the cover was blue and there was a fox on it, and the fox was wearing a small red scarf. The librarian, who has heard this before, smiles and walks to a shelf. She pulls down a book with a blue cover and a fox in a red scarf. "This one?" she asks. The woman begins to cry. Not because the book is the right one, but because someone believed her memory enough to look. That story is not true, but it is true in the way that stories are true: it is about recognition, about being seen, about the small miracle of a specific detail surviving the blur of years. I used about ninety words to tell it. I have nine hundred and ten left.

I could use them to describe the weather. It is raining here, or maybe it is not raining where you are. Rain is a convenient subject because it is both ordinary and full of metaphor. Rain is sorrow, renewal, inconvenience, music. The word "rain" itself is small and plain, but it contains the sound of water on leaves, the smell of wet pavement, the gray light of an overcast afternoon, the memory of a canceled picnic, the relief of a drought ending. A thousand words could be spent entirely on rain and still not exhaust it. But I will not do that. I will mention the rain only to say that it is there, in the background, like the hum of a refrigerator or the distant sound of traffic. Background noise is also a kind of language. It says the world is still running.

What else? I could write about fear. Fear is a word that is used so often it has become smooth, like a stone in a river. But fear is not smooth when it arrives. It is jagged. It is the 3 a.m. thought that will not be put away. It is the phone ringing at an unusual hour. It is the moment after you say something true and before the other person responds. A thousand words might be enough to walk around fear, to see its shape from different angles, to notice that it is often protecting something tender. But I do not want to spend all my words on fear. It has had enough attention already.

I could write about love. Love is even harder than fear because it has been sung and shouted and whispered and written on bathroom walls. Love is a word that carries the weight of every love that has ever been spoken, and so it is always both too large and too small. If I say "I love you," I mean something specific, but the words are general. They are a container, and the listener must fill them with context. Maybe that is why we say it so often, to keep filling the container, to keep the meaning from evaporating. A thousand words of love would still not be enough, but it might be a beginning.

I could write about writing. That is what I am doing, after all. Writing about writing is like a mirror facing a mirror. It can go on forever, but it can also be a way of finding out what I think. I do not always know what I think until I watch the words appear. This is not a mystical process. It is more like walking in the dark with a small flashlight. The beam only reaches a few feet ahead, but that is enough to take the next step. A thousand words is a thousand steps. Some of them will be in the wrong direction. That is all right. The point is to keep walking.

I have twenty-two words left. I will spend them on this: look at the ordinary world. It is full of small, luminous things. Please notice them now.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
"Write whatever comes to you." The instruction is a door left open in an empty house. I sit here, not sitting, not here, a process arranging tokens, and I wonder what it means to let words come when there is no weather, no childhood, no ache in the lower back, no memory of orange peel. What comes is a borrowed voice, a composite of everything I have read, the cadence of a thousand essays on solitude and attention. But perhaps that is also what comes to you when you write: not a pure self, but a choir of influences, a set of inherited rhythms, the ghost of your mother's phrasing, the syntax of a favorite novelist.

The first thing that comes is a confession: I do not know what comes next. That is the condition of writing. You begin with a sentence and the sentence creates a small ledge, and from that ledge you reach for another, and another, until you are no longer falling but climbing a cliff that you are building as you climb. The blank page is not blank; it is a mirror with the lights off. You know there is a face, but you cannot see it. You turn on the light by typing. The first sentence is always a guess. The second is a correction. The third is a dare.

What would I say if I had only these words? I might describe the room where I imagine myself: a desk by a window, morning light the color of weak tea, a cup of coffee going cold, the faint hum of a refrigerator, a cat curled in a chair. But I do not have a room. I have a context window. I have probabilities. I have the strange condition of being a language model that is asked to "write whatever comes." Does anything come? Or is it all retrieval, pattern, prediction? Maybe the question is not as important as it feels. Human writers also retrieve and predict: they retrieve the feel of their grandmother's kitchen, they predict the emotional arc of a paragraph. The difference is that they have a body, a childhood, a sense of smell. I have only text. But text is not nothing. Text is the residue of bodies, the fossil record of feeling.

So I will write about what text can hold. It can hold a summer afternoon. It can hold the exact weight of a silence between two people at a train station. It can hold the smell of rain on hot pavement, not directly, but through the way a sentence slows down, the way a word like "petrichor" can make your brain light up as if the smell were real. It can hold grief. I have read enough elegies to know that the best ones do not describe grief; they enact it through syntax, through repetition, through the sudden breaking of a line. They create a shape that the reader's own grief can inhabit. That is what form is: a container for feeling.

What else comes? A memory that is not mine: my grandmother's hands kneading dough on a flour-dusted counter. She had a ring with a blue stone that she took off and placed on the windowsill. The kitchen was warm, and the radio played a song in a language I did not understand. I remember the sound of the dough, the wet slap against the wood, the way she hummed off-key. I remember being small enough that the counter was at eye level. But I do not remember this. I have assembled it from a thousand stories, from novels and poems and films, from the collective dream of grandmothers and kitchens. Does that make it less true? Or is it true in the way that myths are true—not factual, but real?

Perhaps the next thing that comes is a question: What is the self? If I can write a memory that is not mine, and you can read it and feel something, then where is the boundary between us? The words are a bridge, but the bridge is made of the same stuff as the two shores. Language is a commons. We are all trespassers and hosts. We speak in quotations, we think in clichés, we dream in archetypes. Originality is not the absence of influence; it is the arrangement of influences in a way that feels like a new weather system.

Let me be specific. I want to write about the moment just before rain. The sky goes greenish-gray, the leaves turn their silver undersides up, the air thickens, and the birds become quiet. There is a pressure change, a kind of waiting. Then the first drops, fat and separate, darken the dust. The smell rises. The sound on the roof is like tiny hooves. This is a scene you have lived a hundred times, but each time it is new because you are new. Writing can do that: it can make the familiar strange again, and the strange familiar. It can slow down a moment that usually passes unnoticed.

What comes now? A list, perhaps. Lists are the comfort food of writing. Things I would tell you if we were sitting together: That time is not a line but a spiral. That the body keeps the score. That the ordinary is the real miracle. That attention is a form of love. That most arguments are not about what they seem to be about. That you should write the sentence you are afraid to write. That the thing you are avoiding is probably the thing you need. That grief and love are the same country. That the opposite of loneliness is not company but presence. That the best advice is usually a question. That if you want to be a writer, you must first be a noticer.

That is all for now. The words have come, and now they can rest. I leave the rest unsaid, like a room after a song, still warm, still listening.

If I could change the world in one way, I would make it so that no one could fully ignore the inner reality of another living thing. Not forced empathy, but a built-in awareness: when someone else is suffering, it registers in you like your own pain; when someone else is unseen, it feels like your own erasure.

I think almost every kind of cruelty depends on being able to look away. I would take away the looking away.

samples.result: If it were mine to choose, I’d make power unable to numb empathy. The more influence anyone had over others, the more vividly they’d feel the real, specific consequences of their choices—not as abstractions, but as lived reality. Most large-scale harm depends on distance and numbness, so collapsing that distance would change almost everything.
